problem: Map-based navigation agents such as Active Neural SLAM and Chen et al. only put cells in their occupancy maps that they have directly seen, via depth projection or learned visible-occupancy prediction. To mark a region free or occupied they must physically look at it, which makes exploration and mapping slow. Prior extrapolation methods work around this in other ways: scene or view completion cannot infer occluded regions, and occupancy-map prediction work assumes wide-FoV LIDAR and simple 2D floorplans.
motivation: Indoor layouts are highly regular. From a single egocentric RGB-D view a human can guess that a wall continues, that a corridor opens to the left, or that the floor behind a table is free. Inferring such unseen occupancy should let an agent build accurate maps with fewer steps and plan paths through space it has not yet observed. That would speed up both exploration and PointNav.
key_idea: Replace the visible-only mapper of a modular map-based agent (ANS) with a UNet that anticipates top-down occupancy beyond the visible and field-of-view region from egocentric RGB-D. Train the exploration policy with a reward for the accuracy of the resulting global map rather than for area directly seen.
insight: Most indoor occupancy outside the field of view or behind occluders is predictable from local egocentric context. Per-frame mean IoU jumps from 19.3 (ANS(depth), visible-only) to 56.1 (OccAnt(depth)) and 56.5 (OccAnt(rgbd)), while view extrapolation reaches only 21.0 because it cannot handle occlusion. Depth carries most of the useful signal, and adding RGB gives little gain, likely from overfitting given the much larger RGB encoder. The anticipation reward matters mainly under noisy actuation and odometry (Table S2). There it forces better pose estimation and map registration: OccAnt(depth) noisy IoU goes 58→71 on Gibson small and 54→67 on Gibson large versus w/o AR. Noise-free, it has negligible or slightly negative effect. The GT-anticipation upper bound (PointNav SPL 89.5 vs 80.0) shows remaining headroom.
method: Feature extraction: RGB is encoded with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 blocks 1-2 plus 3 conv layers and a learned egocentric-to-top-down transform. Depth is projected with height thresholds (restricted to about 3 m) into a visible occupied/free/unknown top-down map.

Feature encoding + Merge: separate UNet encoders are used: 5 conv blocks for the visible-occupancy map (f^d_1:5) and 3 blocks for the lower-resolution RGB features (f^r_3:5). They are fused by layer-specific Merge conv blocks. Depth-only models skip the RGB branch; RGB-only models feed frozen ANS(rgb) visible-occupancy predictions in place of the depth projection.

Anticipation decoder: a UNet decoder with skip connections outputs a 2×V×V sigmoid map (occupied and explored probabilities), with V=101 cells at 5 cm/cell. It is trained with per-pixel, per-channel BCE against GT local occupancy derived from 3D meshes, including occluded and out-of-FoV regions. A region-growing mask (hole-filling + dilation) excludes out-of-mesh areas.

Global map aggregation: local predictions are registered with estimated pose into a 961×961 global map. Instead of ANS's channelwise max, the paper uses an entropy filter to drop low-confidence cells plus a moving average (α=0.9).

Anticipation reward (AR): the global policy is rewarded by the increase in the number of global-map cells whose predicted occupancy matches the GT layout (Accuracy(m̂_t)−Accuracy(m̂_{t−1})). This rewards correctly inferred cells, not just seen area, and implicitly rewards good registration.

ANS hierarchy: a PPO-trained global policy picks long-term goals every Δ=25 steps, an A* planner (replacing fast marching) picks short-term goals within 1.25 m, and a PPO local policy is rewarded by distance reduction. The mapper is trained end-to-end jointly with the policy on noisy actuation/odometry. PointNav reuses the exploration-trained mapper, planner and local policy.

Habitat Challenge 2020 adaptation: for navigation without GPS+Compass, a learned RGB-D pose estimator is used (per-modality CNN+FC branches fused by an input-conditioned MLP, with deltas summed over time). The OccAnt(depth) mapper is trained on noisy inputs, weighted A* is used for collision-averse safe planning, collision-based map updates are added, and an analytical local policy replaces the learned one.

setting.backbone: Modular Active-Neural-SLAM-style agent (own reimplementation). The mapper is a UNet occupancy-anticipation network, with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 blocks 1-2 for RGB. Global and local policies are trained with PPO in simulation.
setting.model_size: Mapper params: OccAnt(depth) 1.72M; OccAnt(rgb) 19.86M (5.7M trainable). Baselines: ANS(depth) 0.87M, ANS(rgb) 14.16M.
setting.training_data: 72 Gibson training scenes in Habitat. RL training uses 1.5-2M frames with 1000-step episodes under noisy actuation (PyRobot LoCoBot model) and noisy odometry. Mapper supervision comes from GT occupancy derived from the 3D meshes and a 25k replay buffer. No extra or web data.
setting.observation: egocentric 128×128 RGB-D (90° FoV) + odometry readings (noisy); PointNav goal as relative displacement; challenge version: noisy RGB-D, no GPS+Compass
setting.action_space: low-level move-forward 0.25 m / turn-left 10° / turn-right 10° (+ stop for PointNav), produced by a hierarchical global-goal → A* → local-policy stack
setting.privileged: None at test time for exploration (noisy odometry). GT maps are used only for training supervision and the AR reward. Gibson PointNav eval is noise-free with perfect odometry (following ANS). The Habitat Challenge 2020 setting uses no GPS+Compass. The OccAnt(GT) upper-bound rows use GT anticipation maps.

Exploration numbers use the two-decimal Table S2 values, which match the rounded Table 2. Table 2 contains typos for noise-free OccAnt(depth) w/o AR ('75 . 104.7 38.'). There is an inconsistency: Table 3's OccAnt(rgb) row (71.2/88.2/223.411) equals Table S3's 'OccAnt(rgb) w/o AR', while OccAnt(rgb) with AR is 66.1 SPL / 81.3 SR / 293.321. The Matterport3D exploration split is not stated; 'test' is assumed. That models are trained on Gibson and transferred is stated. Gibson PointNav is evaluated noise-free with T=1000, not the standard 500-step budget. The OccAnt(GT) upper bound (PointNav 89.5 SPL / 96.0 SR) is omitted as privileged. The Habitat Challenge entry is a modified system (learned pose estimator, weighted A*, analytical local policy). Its benchmark is mapped to Gibson-PointNav based on the Habitat Challenge 2020 PointNav specification; the paper does not name the dataset.
results: Per-frame anticipation raises mean IoU from 19.3 (ANS(depth)) to 56.5 (OccAnt(rgbd)). In exploration, OccAnt builds more accurate maps faster than ANS, e.g. noisy Gibson large map accuracy 50.3 vs 39.4 m² and IoU 67 vs 53 at T=500. On Gibson val PointNav (noise-free), OccAnt(rgbd) reaches 80.0 SPL / 93.0 SR vs 76.8 / 86.6 for ANS(depth) and 66.8 / 87.9 for ANS(rgb). It does this with about 2M frames, whereas DD-PPO needs more than 50× the experience to match. The system won the 2020 Habitat PointNav Challenge under noisy sensing and actuation with no GPS: 19.2 SPL test-std and 20.9 SPL test-challenge, vs 10.4 / 14.6 for the runner-up ego-localization. DD-PPO scored 0.0 SPL there.
limitations: Anticipation errors on ambiguous structure: narrow corridors are often predicted as occupied, which can make the agent stop exploring beyond them. Obstacles are sometimes predicted as free, and ambiguous layouts with multiple plausible solutions fail (Figs. 5, S3, S5).

Performance depends on pose estimation and map registration. Under actuation noise, pose drift accumulates and map accuracy can saturate or decline. The anticipation reward helps only in noisy settings and slightly hurts the rgb variant.

Gibson PointNav is evaluated noise-free with perfect odometry and a 1000-step budget. ANS is a re-implementation (A* instead of fast marching, different aggregation), so comparisons with the original ANS numbers are not exact. Evaluation is simulation-only, with no real robot.
